messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh had spent forty years of his life in motion, first as a refugee himself and then, for decades, as a dedicated aid worker, his small van a familiar sight delivering supplies and comfort to newly arrived families. At seventy-two, he was supposed to be slowing down, but the work was his life. That life, however, had ended six months ago on a highway overpass. He was driving a young family to a medical appointment when a repurposed utility truck swerved violently into their lane. The world dissolved into a concussive roar and a flash of white light. Minh remembers nothing more, only disconnected snapshots that ambush him now: the glint of sun on shattered glass suspended in the air, the crimson stain blooming on the passenger seat, the high-pitched shriek of metal. Sometimes, when the house is quiet, he can still hear that shriek, an auditory scar that feels more real than the memory of his own wife’s voice.

In the weeks that followed, these fragments began to govern his life. The intrusive images of the wreck, so vivid and sharp, triggered a terrifying, primal conviction that the danger was not over; it was imminent and everywhere. Sitting in his living room, a picture of the twisted metal would flash in his mind, and his body would respond as if the crash were happening again. His heart would pound, and a cold sweat would break out as he scanned the street outside his window, certain he was being watched. He began to feel that being superalert was the only thing keeping him safe. This constant state of watchfulness, in turn, made the world a minefield of triggers. The rumble of a garbage truck down the street was no longer just a sound; it was the prelude to an explosion, a sensory cue that instantly brought back the sound of the blast and the image of the shattered windshield. The loop was complete and merciless: the memory ignited the threat, and the feeling of threat made the memory inescapable.

The memories also fueled a quiet, corrosive self-assessment. He would sit for hours replaying the moments before the attack, convinced his decision to take the highway instead of the side streets was the fatal error. The thought, *I should have known, I put them in danger*, became a constant, punishing refrain. This self-blame was so consuming that he stopped driving altogether. The driver’s seat of his own car felt like an accusation. At first, his wife, Lien, was understanding, but as weeks turned into months, his refusal to even be a passenger became a significant strain. Any attempt on her part to discuss it, however gently, was met with his immediate retreat. The chaos and violence of the memory had left him with an intense fear of any confrontation, and he would simply leave the room rather than face her worried questions.

His world has now shrunk to the four walls of his house and the small garden out back. This is the only place he feels a semblance of safety. He has taken a leave of absence from the center, unable to bear the thought of getting into a vehicle or the unpredictable noises of the busy city office. Sometimes, when a particularly vivid memory surfaces—the smell of burnt rubber, the impossible angle of the steering wheel—the entire event feels like a fever dream. He has found himself saying to Lien, "It’s so extreme, it’s hard to believe it actually happened to me," as if speaking of a character in a film. But the fear it leaves behind is profoundly real. It was after he found himself hiding in the pantry for an hour because a neighbour’s car had backfired that Lien finally insisted he seek help. Minh agreed, not out of hope, but out of a weary recognition that he could not go on living in a world that had become as small and as frightening as the final, terrifying moments inside his van.
